text: A single number or string is rarely useful on its own. Real data comes in collections: a column of prices, a customer with several attributes, a list of orders. Python gives you four built-in structures for holding collections, and each fits a different job. Even once pandas takes over most of your day-to-day data handling, these four appear constantly underneath it, and data arriving from APIs and JSON files shows up as exactly these structures.

A list holds items in order, written in square brackets — you can add to it, change it, and pick out items by position, counting from zero. Append 42 to a list of totals, and print the first item, the last item using negative-one, and a slice from 1 to 3. A slice like 1-colon-3 includes position 1 and stops before position 3. Handy list methods include append, sort, and len for the count.

A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed after it's created, written in parentheses — use it for a small fixed group of related values, such as a latitude and longitude. Unpacking assigns each element to its own name — lat and lon straight from point — the same trick you used when a function returned several values. Try to change an element, though, and Python raises a TypeError: tuples don't support item assignment.

A dictionary stores values under labels called keys — the natural structure for one record, like a single customer with an id and a name. Square brackets raise a KeyError if the key is missing; dot-get returns None instead, or a default you provide, which is safer when data is incomplete. Add or update a key the same way you'd read one. Loop over customer dot items to get each key and value together.

Put dictionaries in a list and you have a table where each dictionary is a row and each key is a column name. Filter for names where the total is over 50 with a comprehension, and you get Ada and Linus back. This shape matters because it's exactly what JSON from a web API looks like once parsed — Chapter 6 covers that, and pandas can turn this structure straight into a DataFrame.

A set stores each value at most once and doesn't keep order — the quickest way to find the distinct values in a collection and to test membership. Turn a list with a repeated city code into a set, and the duplicate disappears; length tells you the distinct count. Sets also support math: ampersand for items in both, pipe for items in either, and minus for items only in the first one — handy for questions like which customers bought in both months.

Here's a trap that surprises everyone once: assigning a list to a second name does not copy it — both names point at the same list. Set x to a list, set y equal to x, then append to y, and x changes too, because they're the same object in memory. Use dot-copy when you need an independent copy instead. You'll meet this exact idea again with NumPy views in Chapter 2 and pandas DataFrames in Chapter 3.
So how do you choose? Ordered and changeable, reach for a list. A fixed group of values, a tuple. Looking things up by name, a dict. Unique values or overlap questions, a set.

To recap: lists, tuples, dicts, and sets each fit a different job, and a list of dicts is a table in disguise — the shape of JSON data. Dot-get avoids a KeyError, and dot-copy avoids aliasing surprises. Next lesson: errors and debugging.
